AbstractText.Label: CONTEXT
AbstractText.content: Chronic pubalgia affects around 10% of athletes.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To determine the role of pulse-dose radiofrequency (PDRF) in athletes with chronic pubalgia and investigate the causes with imaging.

AbstractText.Label: PATIENTS
AbstractText.content: PDRF was performed on 32 patients with a chronic pain that had been refractory to conservative therapies during the last 3 mo.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTION
AbstractText.content: The genital branches of the genitofemoral, ilioinguinal, and iliohypogastric nerves and the obturator nerve were the goals of treatment. A 10-cm, 20-gauge cannula was inserted with a percutaneous access on the upper and lower edges of the iliopubic branch. After the spindle was removed, a radiofrequency needle with a 10-mm "active tip" was inserted. The radiofrequency technique was performed with 1200 pulses at 45 V and 20-ms duration, followed by a 480-ms silent phase.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
AbstractText.content: The follow-up with a clinical examination was performed at 1, 3, 6, and 9 mo after the procedure. During the follow-up visits, the patients were asked to rate their pain on a 0-10 VAS scale.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: All of the enrolled patients completed the study. Mean VAS score before the treatment was 8.4 ± 0.6. Twenty-four patients had a reduction of pain VAS scores more than 50% during all follow-up visits and started training and physiotherapy in the days after the radiofrequency procedure. Six patients, each treated 2 times, had a reduction more than 50% of VAS scores and could start training and physiotherapy only after the 2nd procedure. One patient had no pain relief with 2 treatments. Pain intensity decreased up to 9 mo in 31 patients (mean VAS scores 3.4 ± 0.5 at 6 mo and 3.8 ± 0.9 at 9 mo). No complications were observed.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: PDRF is an effective and safe technique in management of chronic pubalgia in athletes.

Article.ArticleTitle: Pulse-Dose Radiofrequency in Athletic Pubalgia: Preliminary Results.
